newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian communists await Castro with awe.
newsitem.headline: Italian communists await Castro with awe.

text.p: Vezio Bagazzini points to a battered card on a shelf behind the bar where he serves lunchtime coffee and aperitifs and a flush of pride lights his face.
"I have this visiting card -- they say it's authentic," he explains. It reads Fidel Castro Ruz, President of the Council of State and of the Government, Republic of Cuba.

Castro, the world's longest serving communist leader and icon of the international left, is expected in Rome in the early hours of Friday for a World Food Summit, setting off a frenzy of anticipation among his admirers in Italy.

Bagazzini's tiny bar on a cobbled street in the heart of Rome is a shrine to all things Marxist. Red flags line the walls, a bust of Lenin stands on a shelf and a poster of Che Guevara hangs from the ceiling.
A visit from the "lider maximo" (great leader) would be the icing on the cake for Bagazzini, a life-long communist in a country that once boasted the biggest Marxist party in the West.
"I may be a bit presumptuous but I really hope someone brings him here, it would be the greatest thing," he said.
"I think he's a charismatic figure...the last testimony in the flesh of another social system," he told Reuters. "The Chinese are red capitalists...only the Cubans have remained."
Diplomatic sources say Castro is scheduled to address the summit at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation's (FAO) Rome headquarters on Friday and will meet Italian leaders.
He was appointed one of the summit's six vice-chairmen at its opening session on Wednesday.
All eyes will be on whether Castro, an atheist whose regime has sometimes testy relations with the Roman Catholic Church, also has an historic meeting with Pope John Paul.
A group of exiled Cubans plans to lobby Castro and have staged a "pilgrimage of pain" from the United States to the Vatican to protest against alleged human rights abuses in Cuba.
They attended the Pope's general audience at the Vatican on Wednesday. "I pray for Cuba every day," the Pontiff told one member of the group, wheelchair-bound Dalia Santana, 81.
Castro's movements, as ever, are shrouded in secrecy.
"When the plane lands," was the answer given by one Cuban diplomat when asked by a reporter this week when it would be known for certain whether the 70-year-old leader would come.
FAO director general Jacques Diouf said on Wednesday Castro would travel to Rome for the summit but he did not know when.
The Communist daily Il Manifesto is already planning to fete the visit with a special supplement of the official Cuban newspaper Granma and to carry a column signed by Castro himself.
Italy's communist party, which could command one in three votes at its height 20 years ago, was disbanded in 1991 when it relaunched as a social democratic force.

However, ex-communists are the backbone of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government, the first to include the left in almost 50 years, and Prodi relies on the hardline Communist Refoundation party for a majority in parliament.
One Italian woman out shopping suggested it was time Castro reformed his own politics.
"He seems a bit left behind historically," she said.
"He's a poor old man," echoed Antonio Sternativo from the southern town of Francavilla Fontana. "I have nothing against Castro -- he's a symbol of the past, innocuous," he said.

But Mario Laurenti, an office worker who attended a rally in Rome aged 14 to mark the first anniversary of the 1967 shooting of Marxist guerrilla Ernesto "Che" Guevara by Bolivian troops, said Castro's visit should "relaunch the image of Cuba and pose the problem of the embargo, which is absurd by now".
The United States imposed economic and trade sanctions against Cuba in 1962 to try to force Castro out.
